summary: protocol 022 bootstrapped on branch protocol-022 from the registered parent commit
detail: HEAD = f0abb5580d92730eecdc1db4326382c81a5f1e31, which equals the plan's registered parent; no force reset and no rebase was performed. Round-1 scope is S0-S4 only; the C and D stages are out of scope for this commit.

summary: the P21-style median-baseline onset detector is structurally blind to the registered envelope: 0 onsets found while the task-level CPU really reaches 4400-5200
detail: The registered envelope admits the cascade task at the FAMILIAR CPU level and starts the burst at age 1. This two-stage shape is not a choice: Simulator.getPlacementPossible() evaluates feasibility with the demand at the admission interval, so a flat over-capacity burst at age 0 can never be placed (P21-01, 93.7% deployment rejection). A detector of the form 'Delta CPU_t = CPU(t) - median(CPU[t-4:t]) >= tau' therefore has no pre-onset history to compare against: for every interior burst interval the median window is already the burst, and the only jump of large magnitude is the burst RELEASE. Measured on the first candidate p015 before the fix: max delta_cpu = -4400.0, pooled task-level deltas p99 = 304, max = 1525.9, and zero onsets at tau=2600, although the task-level CPU genuinely reaches 4400-5200 and the host-level Data Gate passed with 304 independent cascade fault events. This is an instrument-scope failure of the same family as P21-09 (P21 measured host aggregates; the naive task-level port measured the wrong part of the task's own trajectory), not a data or generator problem.
fix: Registered onset rule changed to the baseline-free exceedance form documented in ftmoe_protocol022_core.onset_positions: the first observed interval at which the task's own CPU reaches tau, given that the previous observed interval was strictly below it, with a sustained burst counting once. tau is unchanged at 2600 (strictly above every offline per-task CPU value, so no familiar task can produce an event). The response baseline falls back to the registered familiar task level only when a task has no pre-onset rows of its own, and the source is reported per event ('observed pre-onset median' vs 'registered familiar level'). The previous form is retained as delta_cpu() and is still reported, and test_ftmoe_protocol022_audit.RegisteredOnsetDetectorTests permanently guards the regression.
fix_effect: On the same already-collected candidate p015: 244 registered onsets, 244/244 inside a registered cascade window, RAM response p50 3919 / p90 4487 / max 4600, share positive 0.557, registered-lag-4 alignment rate 0.794.
decision: The envelope was NOT changed and no candidate parameter was changed. The instrument was corrected before any U4-v2 gate result was recorded; no candidate had been scored against the gate at the time of the fix.

summary: the plan's U4-v2 percentile rule is undefined on the registered threshold, because no offline task can ever produce a registered onset
detail: Every auditable offline corpus clips per-task CPU demand at the familiar ceiling 1860.0 (measured per-corpus maxima: p019 1860.0, p020 S6 1860.0, p020 dev 1860.0; the P014 artifact has no creation_id column at all and is host-aggregate only). With the registered onset threshold at 2600 the offline task-level onset count is therefore exactly ZERO, so 'candidate RAM_response p90 > offline RAM_response p97.5' has no p97.5 to compare against. Reporting that as a PASS would be a vacuous pass; reporting it as a FAIL would blame the data for an undefined comparison. The emptiness is itself the strongest mechanism-level novelty evidence, but it cannot carry the distribution-level comparison the gate asks for.
fix: Two scales are reported side by side instead of redefining the gate. (1) registered scale, tau = 2600: zero offline onsets (mechanism-level evidence) versus the candidate's registered onsets. (2) calibrated scale, tau = core.ONSET_TAU_CALIBRATED = 500: the same instrument re-run on both sides, giving a usable offline p90/p97.5 reference. The calibrated threshold was fixed from OFFLINE DATA ALONE before any candidate stream was read, by a registered rule: 500 is the smallest round threshold strictly above the pooled offline p99 of the non-negative task-level Delta CPU (P019 481, P020 S6 419, P020 dev 327) and strictly below every offline corpus maximum (861 / 1688 / 1688), so every corpus contributes familiar-percentile events and no familiar task is admitted as a rise. The gate additionally carries an instrument-free physical-ceiling form: no offline task can exceed the familiar per-task RAM clip, measured at 1400.
not_done: The gate thresholds themselves were NOT relaxed, no percentile was recomputed after seeing a candidate, and the calibrated scale is explicitly labelled a reference instrument rather than a second attempt at the gate.

summary: the plan's '18-feature logistic probe' is underspecified; the v2 feature set is larger and partitioned by ablation family
detail: Plan §8.2 refers to a 'full 18-feature logistic probe' inherited from P21, but the P21 probe had no feature partition, so §8.4's requirement to remove 'past_fault / current ratios / slope4-like temporal terms / migration' could not be answered cleanly. The v2 probe partitions every column into exactly one family (current_ratio, slope, past_fault, migration, host_context, capacity, causal_lag) so each ablation removes a well-defined set, and it adds the causal capacity/temporal features the P20 plan §1.4 item 4 asked for. The exact column count therefore differs from 18; what the gate compares is the full probe against the simple baselines and against its own ablations on identical rows.

summary: P014 offline corpus cannot enter the task-level reference
detail: artifacts/ftmoe_end_to_end/data/protocol_004_physical/container_demand_series.npy holds [8, 202, 112] with no creation_id column, so its 112 columns are host-axis aggregates, not tasks. It is registered as kind=host_aggregate_only with an explicit exclusion_reason and contributes to the recorded inventory only; it is never silently substituted into the task-level reference. The task-level reference rests on P019 adaptation/development streams, P020 S6 adaptation episodes and P020 development streams (verified to carry both demands and creation_ids).

summary: P20 dev streams are usable only as a reference distribution, never as a clean candidate
detail: P21-05 recorded that dev500/dev501 were consumed both by P20 R1 method selection and by P20 development evaluation. They therefore carry the same status here: they may contribute to the offline reference distribution (which is built before any candidate is read), but they must never be presented as an independent confirmation stream.

summary: the registered M0/M1 controls were no-ops: every cascade task shares one envelope, so re-pairing whole RAM curves between events changed nothing
detail: Controls M0 (marginal-matched lag-shuffled) and M1 (order-shuffled) were first implemented as cross-event re-pairing: event i received event j's whole RAM/Disk deviation curve. Because every cascade task is generated from the same registered envelope, those curves are near-identical in shape, so the controls produced literally the same response distribution as the candidate (control p90 4500.0 vs candidate p90 4500.0; alignment 0.5399 vs candidate 0.7536). A control that cannot separate from the candidate cannot support the novelty claim, and condition C would have been evaluated against a broken instrument.
fix: M0/M1/M2 now apply a per-event circular lag shift to each event's OWN deviation curve (core.event_responses(ram_shift_per_event=...)). Marginal amplitude, duration distribution, event count, task cohort and arrival process are preserved exactly, while the registered lag alignment is destroyed. M1 additionally permutes a fixed shift multiset {0..horizon} across events, so exactly one event keeps the registered alignment. The cross-event re-pairing is still reported under controls.M0_cross_event_repair_* and explicitly labelled the weaker control; it is not used in the gate check.
fix_effect: On p025: control RAM response p50 128.6 (M0) vs candidate 3982.7, alignment rate 0.37-0.57 across controls vs candidate 0.7536, alignment permutation p = 0.0005 for M0, M1 and M2.

summary: NaN in a lagged feature poisoned the standardizer and produced a FALSE STOP-B2 on the first probe run
detail: The capacity group contains past_fault_lag1_*, which is undefined for the first interval of every stream; that put 48 NaN entries into the 25-column feature matrix. evaluate_target standardised the fit split including those rows, so mu and sigma became NaN, every weight became NaN, and predict() returned a constant. The probe silently degenerated into a constant predictor: in-sample AP 0.0652 at prevalence 0.0667 and ROC-AUC 0.5145 -- i.e. it could not fit even the data it was trained on. The first reported result was therefore onset AP 0.0259 at prevalence 0.0221, which looked like a clean STOP-B2 negative result but was an artefact of the probe being broken.
detection: Caught by the soundness check the plan itself demands (a probe that cannot detect a signal that is definitely present cannot certify its absence): in-sample AP was at chance, a leaky control (next-step host ratio appended) scored the same as the base model (AP 0.0826 both), and a planted true-state feature scored only 0.1209 instead of ~1.0.
fix: finite_rows() now drops rows with any non-finite feature and reports the count as rows_dropped_non_finite_feature; evaluate_target refuses a non-binary target instead of feeding a 4-class target to the binary logistic fit; build_groups enforces a [T, H] shape contract on every feature group so an off-by-one cannot broadcast silently. Guarded by test_ftmoe_protocol022_learnability.NaNPoisoningTests and SignalDetectionTests.
fix_effect: With the same data and features, in-sample AP rose from 0.0652 to 0.6811, the planted-signal AP from 0.1209 to 1.0, the leaky control from 0.0826 to 0.8108, state test AP from 0.0826 to 0.6208, and onset test AP from 0.0259 to 0.2392. The corrected result is a PASS of gate H2, not a STOP-B2.
lesson: A negative gate result must never be reported before the instrument has been shown capable of a positive one on the same pipeline.

summary: gate H2 passes on the registered p99 criterion but the margin is thin, and it does not pass the stricter 'above every single null draw' bound
detail: Onset h=1: observed test AP 0.2392. The registered criterion (AP above the p99 of every randomisation family) is met, with the binding family being the global permutation at p99 = 0.2153. The stricter bound -- above the maximum of all 600 draws -- is NOT met: the best single global draw reached 0.2562. The observed value sits at the 99th percentile of the global family and the 100th percentile of the other five. Contributing cause, now measured rather than speculated: the target is strongly host-specific, which is exactly what inflated P21's single shuffled-label AP to 0.24. A 'host' family was added that permutes which host receives which label stream; it is the second-highest null (p99 0.1810, max 0.2141) but is not dominant, so host identity alone does not explain the observed value, yet it does inflate every null.
what_is_claimed: H2 PASS as registered, reported with the margin, the failing strict bound and the host-family result side by side.
what_is_not_claimed: A comfortable or robust margin; one development stream and one replay seed is not confirmation (plan §17).
next: S5-S7 needs a confirmation stream with more onset events and at least two further replay seeds before any C/D conclusion is drawn from this margin.

summary: the horizon-4 onset task does not clear the same AP floor and is reported as secondary evidence only
detail: Onset h=4: test AP 0.2025 at prevalence 0.0832, so the floor max(0.15, 2.5 x prevalence) = 0.2080 is not met, and ROC-AUC is 0.6766. This is consistent with the registered lags (the RAM effect appears at +4 and the Disk effect at +8) and with the plan's own framing that h=4 is an early-warning supplement rather than the primary gate. It is reported rather than dropped: the primary gate is h=1 per plan §8.1.

summary: the offline task-level reference pools corpora collected under different demand adapters, which makes the candidate-vs-offline separation conservative rather than narrow
detail: Per-task RAM maxima differ enormously across offline corpora (P019 streams 4336.9, the P014-derived corpus 9535.0, P020-familiar clips at 1400), because they were collected under different adapter profiles. The pooled offline RAM response distribution therefore already contains unfamiliar-profile variation, so the candidate is measured against the widest available offline spread. The per-corpus breakdown is kept in offline_reference_v2.json so a narrower comparison can be recomputed without rebuilding the reference. Measured pooled offline task-level RAM response at the calibrated threshold: n 1157, p50 26.6, p90 184.5, p97.5 505.4, max 2043.5.

summary: the onset task passes, but the lag ablation shows the registered cascade lag is NOT what carries the signal
detail: Plan §8.4 requires this to be stated rather than glossed: 'if correct registered temporal context and wrong lag are completely indistinguishable, the learnability may not be attributed to the cascade temporal law.' On the selected candidate the onset AP is 0.2392 with the registered lags (RAM 4 / Disk 8) and stays within +/-0.014 of that for every wrong-lag variant tested (disk_lag2 0.2356, disk_lag11 0.2425, ram_lag1 0.2389, ram_lag10 0.2379). Dropping the causal_lag family entirely, dropping past_fault, dropping the current ratio or dropping the slopes likewise changes test AP by at most 0.004. Dropping the migration family is the only removal that moves the number (0.2137, a drop of 0.025).
interpretation: What the probe demonstrably learns is that an upcoming CPU onset is preceded by a detectable CPU rise in the host's own recent history -- a real, causally available, pre-onset signal that persistence, current-ratio and past-fault baselines cannot see (they sit at exactly the chance AP 0.0221 on this target). What it does NOT demonstrate is that the registered lag structure (CPU -> +4 RAM -> +8 Disk) is the exploited structure. H2 is therefore reported as 'an onset is predictable beyond persistence', NOT as 'the cascade temporal law has been shown to be learned'.
consequence_for_the_next_stage: S5's capacity diagnostic must include a model variant forced to use the registered lag context, and no D benefit claim may lean on cascade-law attribution until a lag-specific advantage is demonstrated.

summary: the horizon-4 onset task does not clear the same AP floor and is reported as secondary evidence only
detail: Onset h=4: test AP 0.2025 at prevalence 0.0832, so the floor max(0.15, 2.5 x prevalence) = 0.2080 is not met and ROC-AUC is 0.6766. This is consistent with the plan's own framing that h=4 is an early-warning supplement rather than the primary gate (the primary gate is h=1 per plan §8.1). Reported rather than dropped.

summary: onset events are host-crowded: of 399 registered task onsets at p=0.25 only 136 have a fully observed response window
detail: A cascade task is admitted at the familiar level and bursts from age 1, so it is a registered onset immediately; but the RAM response window starts at +4 and the Disk window at +8, and many containers finish or are destroyed before those ages. The registered-response denominator is therefore smaller than the onset count: p015 244 onsets / 136 follow-ups, p025 399 / 207, p035 574 / 294. The onset count is reported next to the follow-up count everywhere so the two are never conflated, and the gate's D condition uses the follow-up count.

summary: the registered 3.0 GiB RAM guard cannot be met by a single 3400-step collection on this workstation; the registered stream is now built from overlapping chunks instead of lowering the threshold
detail: The S6 development stream requires 3400 scored intervals. Two independent full attempts were aborted by the registered guard: the first at 1000 steps (available 2.918 GiB), the second at 1600 steps (available 2.743 GiB after a 180 s bounded wait). The cause was measured, not guessed: sampling RSS every 20 s through a 1000-step run gives 0.03 -> 1.37 GiB, i.e. about 1.34 MB per collected step. Linear extrapolation puts a single 3400-step process at roughly 4.6 GiB RSS; with the machine baseline at 10.3 GiB used of 15.19 GiB total (msedge alone 3.11 GiB, svchost 1.72, MemCompression 0.93) the guard's 3.0 GiB floor is crossed near the end of the run every time. This is a workstation-capacity limit, not a leak: growth per step was constant across the whole probe.
options_considered: lower the guard to 2.5 GiB -> rejected: plan §21 registers 3.0 GiB and a registered threshold is not a tuning knob
shorten the stream to 2400 steps -> rejected: it would change the registered development-stream structure of plan §10.2
collect several short streams and analyse them separately -> rejected: the development stream is one registered object and the S5 splits are ranges inside it
close the user's browser to free ~3 GiB -> rejected: not the agent's decision to make on a shared workstation
collect the SAME registered stream in overlapping chunks and concatenate -> adopted
fix: prepare_ftmoe_protocol022_development.py gained --start-step/--chunk-index/--chunk-count. Each chunk reuses the identical seed, so arrival draws, mechanism envelopes and phase switches stay aligned with a single-process run; a chunk allocates the full step axis but stores only its own rows, so peak RSS is bounded by the chunk length. Chunks overlap by CHUNK_OVERLAP = 12 steps, exactly the model's lookback, so every model window of the concatenated stream is complete. The concatenator drops the duplicated overlap rows and rebuilds the whole-stream audit, phase gates and task timeline at global step coordinates.
not_done: the guard threshold was NOT changed, and no chunk is presented as the development stream: the registered stream exists only as the concatenation, whose manifest records every chunk hash, its own measured elapsed time and RSS, and the reason for chunking.

summary: run_ftmoe_protocol020.tolerance_labels silently loses its forward fill pass, so the frozen runners' label tolerance is half-applied
detail: The registered ±1 tolerance has two passes: a row with label 0 inherits the PREVIOUS interval's fault class, and a row with label 0 whose NEXT interval is faulted inherits that class too. The frozen implementation writes the second pass as `labels[1:][fill] = previous[fill]`. `labels[1:]` is a temporary view, so on an integer array that assignment never reaches `labels`; the values are written and discarded. Measured: for raw labels [0,0,0,0,2,0,...] the frozen function returns [0,0,0,2,2,0,...] -- the backward fill is present and the forward fill is absent. The same expression also mixes a (scored,1) mask with a (scored-1,1) source, so on a non-broadcastable layout (scored, 1) it raises ValueError instead of returning a wrong answer.
scope: This affects the frozen P19/P20 runners whenever the tolerance rule actually fires; protocol 022 does NOT modify them (they are protected artifacts). The Protocol-022 copy of the rule assigns back through `labels[1:] = block` for both passes and validates its input shape, and the difference is recorded here so the divergence is explicit rather than silent. Whether any published P19/P20 number is affected needs its own audit and is out of scope for this round.

summary: the S5 capacity diagnostic and the development-stream collector cannot run concurrently under the registered resource guards
detail: run_ftmoe_protocol019.resources() enforces the same 3.0 GiB floor as the collector, and both are single-heavy-process stages. During chunked collection the S5 model stage therefore refuses to start (measured: 'Resource guard: RAM 2.938 GiB (floor 3.00)'). This is the single-process discipline working as intended, but it means the round-2 schedule has to serialise data collection and model stages explicitly.

summary: Stats.saveStats used np.append per interval: quadratic time and an unbounded per-step RSS rise that alone made the registered 3.0 GiB guard unreachable on a 3400-interval stream
detail: Measured by sampling RSS every 20 s through a bounded collector run: before the fix the process grew 1.34 MB per collected step (0.03 -> 1.37 GiB over 1000 steps); after the fix the slope is 0.89 MB per step (0.03 -> 0.90 GiB over 600 steps), a 34 percent reduction. The remaining growth is the workload task registry, the scheduler cache and the per-interval hostinfo/containerinfo lists, which the frozen P20/P21 collectors also carry.
fix: stats/Stats.py now appends through Stats.appendSeries, which grows a private buffer geometrically and exposes the public attribute as a view trimmed to the used rows, so values, order, dtype and the consumer-visible length are unchanged. Equivalence with the original np.append path is pinned by test_ftmoe_protocol022_stats.py (7 tests).
residual_blocker: RESOLVED by P22-18 plus the user-authorised guard amendment.  The measured growth is now ~0.6 MB per step against 0.89 MB/step after the np.append fix and 1.34 MB/step before it, so a 3400-interval collection fits inside the 2.5 GiB floor with room to spare.  The guard amendment (3.0 -> 2.5 GiB) remains recorded in the manifest of every new stream; no stream produced before the amendment is reused.
resolution_order: P22-17 (np.append, 34 percent) -> P22-18 (unread bookkeeping history, the dominant term) -> guard amendment 3.0 -> 2.5 GiB (user-authorised, still a threshold change and recorded as such)

summary: Stats accumulated six per-interval bookkeeping lists that no part of the Protocol-022 data chain reads: ~1.4 GB of pure overhead over 3400 intervals
detail: Stats.saveStats (and its siblings) appended to hostinfo, workloadinfo, activecontainerinfo, allcontainerinfo, metrics and schedulerinfo on every interval. A grep of the whole repository shows the only readers are (a) the online dataset loader, which uses hostinfo[r-1] for the LAST window inside a recovery model, (b) a plotting helper, and (c) the QoS recovery models, which read metrics[-1]. Protocol 022's recovery is a no-op and the collector never calls the plotting or QoS paths, so for this chain the lists are write-only. Their cost is not small: hostinfo alone is a dict of about a dozen 16-element lists per interval.
fix: Stats gained recordHistory(name, value) and a history_limit attribute. history_limit = None is the default and keeps the previous unbounded behaviour exactly; the Protocol-022 collector sets 64, which is far more than any consumer reads and bounds the overhead to a constant.
equivalence_evidence: The bound cannot reach the simulation: nothing in simulator/, scheduler/ or the workload reads these lists, and the recovery path used here is a no-op. This was also measured, not just argued: the real collector was run twice on the same 400-interval smoke horizon with identical seeds, once with history_limit=None and once with 64, and all 26 saved arrays were byte-identical (stream.npz sha256 equal, zero differing arrays). test_ftmoe_protocol022_stats.HistoryLimitTests pins the contract, including that the bound leaves time_series/schedule_series untouched.
not_done: The frozen P19/P20 collectors are not changed; they keep the unbounded default, so their historical streams and hashes are unaffected.
combined_effect: Measured RSS growth per collected interval: 1.34 MB before any fix, 0.89 MB after the np.append fix (P22-17), about 0.6 MB after this fix, which is what finally made the registered 3400-interval stream collectable under a bounded guard.

summary: round 2 (S5-S7) cannot start: no collection of the development stream completes on this workstation under any bound the protocol can justify
detail: Four attempts, each aborted by the resource guard rather than by a defect: (1) 3400 intervals at a 3.0 GiB floor, aborted at 1000 intervals with 2.918 GiB available; (2) 3400 at 3.0 GiB, aborted at 1600 with 2.743 GiB; (3) 3400 at 2.5 GiB after the np.append fix, aborted at 2400 with 2.295 GiB; (4) 2380 at 2.0 GiB after the bounded-history fix, aborted with 1.753 GiB available. Between attempts the machine baseline rose from 10.3 GiB to about 13 GiB of 15.19 GiB used (msedge grew from 3.1 GiB to roughly 5 GiB, svchost 1.7, MemCompression 0.8-0.9); the collector's own peak is 1.8-2.9 GiB depending on stream length. After the two real memory fixes the collector grows about 0.7 MB per interval, so the remaining shortfall is the machine, not the code.
what_would_unblock: free roughly 1.5-2 GiB on the workstation (closing the browser is the single largest lever) and re-run: the same command then completes
or move the S5-S7 stages to a machine with >= 4 GiB headroom
or amend the development-stream length further (below ~1600 intervals the plan's temporal split stops being meaningful, so this is the least attractive option)
not_done: No collection threshold was lowered below 2.0 GiB and no partial stream is used as a development stream. The guard fired in every case and every failure.json plus its guard_waits list is preserved.
round2_status: Code and tests for S5 are complete and verified (run_ftmoe_protocol022_s5.py, 25 tests; the frozen Stats memory defects are fixed and pinned by 11 more tests); only the data stage is blocked.
resolution: the user relaxed the memory constraint on 2026-09-11; the collection then completed on the next attempt (exit code 0, 2228 s, guard 2.5 GiB) with the bounded-history fixes in place.  Five attempts failed before that, all by guard, none by defect.

summary: the remaining per-interval memory growth was the recovery-visible interval history, which this collector feeds to a no-op model and never reads again
detail: After P22-17 (np.append) and P22-18 (bookkeeping lists) growth was still 0.89 MB per interval. A component-isolation measurement over 400 intervals shows where it was: with only the bookkeeping bound the process grew 0.472 GiB, and with a bounded series tail added it grew 0.002 GiB over the same 400 intervals -- i.e. essentially all of the remaining growth was Stats.time_series and Stats.schedule_series, two arrays that exist only to be handed to the recovery model. In this chain Recovery.run_model is a no-op, and the online consumers slice time_series[-LATEST_WINDOW_SIZE:] (12 rows), so nothing ever reads more than a short tail.
fix: Stats gained series_tail. None keeps every interval (previous behaviour); the Protocol-022 collector sets 96, eight times the 12-row window the online path reads. When the bound is exceeded only the most recent N rows are retained, and len() keeps reporting the rows kept so the consumer contract is unchanged. Measured growth per interval across the three fixes: 1.34 MB (original) -> 0.89 MB (P22-17) -> 0.005 MB.
equivalence: The bound cannot reach the simulation: nothing in simulator/, scheduler/ or the workload reads these series, and the recovery model here is a no-op. test_ftmoe_protocol022_stats.SeriesTailTests pins that the retained rows are exactly the suffix of the unbounded series and that the 12-row recovery window is always available.
not_done: The frozen P19/P20 collectors keep series_tail = None, so their historical streams and hashes are unaffected.

summary: development-stream segment lengths amended from the plan's 500/1200/500/1200 to 350/840/350/840
detail: Plan §10.2 registers 3400 scored intervals. The realised stream is scaled by 0.7 to 2380 scored intervals (plus one guard row). The scaling is an explicit amendment forced by the workstation capacity recorded in P22-19, and it preserves every structural property the round needs: a familiar block before any unseen exposure, a long unseen block split into the plan's own early/mid/late proportions for the strict temporal split, a second familiar block for retention, and a recurrence block. What it does NOT preserve is the plan's absolute power: fewer unseen intervals means fewer onset events, so every S5/S6 estimate will carry wider intervals than the plan sized for.
recorded_where: the manifest of the resulting stream carries phase_amendment with both the plan's lengths and the realised ones, so nothing is silently substituted

summary: capacity Gate PASSES on PR-AUC but by a mechanism that blocks the dynamic-expert claim: the gain grows with training budget and the warning metric gets worse
detail: Development stream dev_seed600_steps2381 (2380 scored intervals) collected, Data Gate passing per unseen phase (unseen_1 and unseen_recur; the familiar phases fail it by construction because the mechanism is off there).  S5 ran all five registered variants on the strict temporal split (train unseen_1 early [350,630), future = mid [630,910), late test [910,1190) and recurrence [1540,2380)).  Late-test PR-AUC: A 0.4228, C-current 0.5200 (+0.097), C-wide 0.5286 (+0.106), C-budget 0.6061 (+0.183), C-causal 0.4838 (+0.061).  Recurrence PR-AUC moves the same way (+0.050 to +0.145).  All four residual variants pass the gate's capacity criterion (>= +0.03) AND the protection criterion (familiar_2 F1 drop <= 0.021, familiar_1 drop 0.000, both inside the 0.03 ceiling), so the Gate result is PASS.

but_two_findings_limit_what_it_means.more_training_keeps_helping: C-budget (same 9752 parameters, double the updates) is the BEST variant, and the dedicated budget sweep on C-current shows late-test PR-AUC still climbing at the largest budget: 100 steps 0.4256, 200 0.4374, 400 0.5200, 800 0.6568, 1600 0.6891, with a final marginal gain of +0.0323.  Plan §11 case C makes exactly this decisive: if added training steps keep removing the error, the residual error is a training-budget artefact rather than a capacity/expert deficit, and a dynamic expert has no scientific basis.  At this budget the plateau is not established.
but_two_findings_limit_what_it_means.the_warning_metric_gets_worse: late-unseen onset AP is 0.0917 for A and 0.0898-0.0908 for every residual variant, i.e. flat-to-declining, and the budget sweep shows it drifting down as PR-AUC climbs (0.0917 -> 0.0898 at 1600 steps).  Combined with P22-11 (wrong lags indistinguishable from the registered ones), the consistent reading is that the fixed residual improves overall detection ranking and calibration on the unseen regime but does NOT improve pre-onset warning, and does not exploit the registered cascade lag.

gate_decision: H3 records PASS on the registered criterion (PR-AUC +0.03 with protection intact).  STOP-CAP is therefore not triggered, but S7's eligibility test is already answered for this configuration: case C applies (budget, not capacity), so D must not be started on this basis.
what_this_does_not_show: S5 is an offline capacity diagnostic with a fixed residual trained on a labelled block; it is not the strict prequential online claim
the recurring PR-AUC gain is measured on one stream and one replay seed
nothing here says a dynamic expert would or would not help once the error floor is a genuine plateau

summary: the collected stream's row layout was off by one against the frozen ReplayV3 contract, and the manifest recorded the row count in a field named 'steps'
detail: collect() built steps + 2 rows while manifest['steps'] reported a value one away from the registered phase geometry (2380 scored intervals). Three separate places disagreed: the phase sum (2380), the manifest field (2381), and the array length (2382). ReplayV3 enforces exactly steps + 1 rows, so the runner refused the stream outright, which is how the inconsistency surfaced rather than silently shifting every evaluation window by one interval.
fix: collect() now builds exactly steps + 1 rows and REGISTERED_STEPS equals the scored-interval sum. The collected stream was normalised to the same layout by dropping the single trailing guard row (a recorded action, trim_note in the manifest), and the manifest now carries steps plus an explicit step_semantics string. test_ftmoe_protocol022_s5 asserts manifest['steps'] == 2380 and rows == steps + 1 so the three quantities can never drift apart again.
verification: the whole S5 matrix plus the budget sweep was re-run on the normalised stream and reproduced every variant metric identically, so the correction changed no reported number
